title: 25.5 A 99.5mW/Port DC-to-40GHz Integrated Channel Analyzer for High-Density Signal Integrity Measurement in 28nm CMOS
problem: High-speed electrical links (PCB traces, coaxial cables) in dense Ethernet switches and high-performance computers suffer from reflection, crosstalk, and insertion loss; traditional VNAs and sampling oscilloscopes are power-hungry, expensive, and inefficient.
method: Integrated channel analyzer (ICA) ASIC in 28nm CMOS using time-domain reflectometry (TDR) and time-domain transmission (TDT) techniques for SI measurements. 4-port prototype achieves DC-to-40GHz frequency range with 9.1ps rise time and only 99.5mW per port (398mW total).

title: Cassandra: Efficient Enforcement of Sequential Execution for Cryptographic Programs
problem: Modern out-of-order processors violate constant-time programming assumptions by transiently executing unintended control-flow paths, enabling Spectre-class transient execution attacks against cryptographic code. Existing mitigations that address control-flow misspeculations impose high performance overhead by broadly restricting speculative execution.
method: Cassandra disables branch prediction for constant-time cryptographic code regions and instead records and replays the deterministic sequential control flow using a Branch Trace Unit (BTU) added to the processor. Exploiting the observation that constant-time programs have mostly static control flow across runs and that cryptographic programs are loop-intensive with highly compressible control-flow patterns, Cassandra performs upfront branch analysis to compress control-flow traces stored in the BTU. The BTU then supplies fetch redirections from compressed trace storage, bypassing speculative branch prediction entirely for protected code regions.

title: SPAD Flash LiDAR with Chopped Analog Counter for 76m Range and 120klx Background Light
problem: Flash LiDAR using single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) must simultaneously achieve long range (76m), high depth resolution, and high frame rates under strong background light (120klx) without performance degradation.
method: Direct time-of-flight (dToF) sensor using SPADs with chopped analog counter architecture that suppresses background-light interference and enables 76m range with high frame-rate histogramming at 120klx ambient light.

title: Late Breaking Results: Automated Topology Generation for Power Amplifier Designs through BiLSTM-based DNN and Multi-objective Optimizations
problem: Power amplifier (PA) design requires selecting optimal circuit topology (matching networks) and hyperparameters; manual design is time-consuming and requires extensive expertise in RF circuit design.
method: The approach uses a BiLSTM (bidirectional long short-term memory) deep neural network to classify and predict the optimal PA topology for a given HEMT device. Multi-objective Pareto front-based optimization refines the DNN hyperparameters (hidden layers, neurons). The method is validated on GaN HEMT designs, generating PAs with 40 dBm power output, 50%+ power-added efficiency (PAE), and >10 dB gain.

title: MEGA.mini: A Universal Generative AI Processor with a New Big/Little Core Architecture for NPU
problem: Generative AI processors must efficiently accelerate both non-diffusion models (VAEs, GANs, transformers) and diffusion models; diffusion models require 25–100x more operations due to iterative inference, creating a computational mismatch for single-architecture designs.
method: MEGA.mini implements a big/little core architecture where big cores optimize for NDM inference (CNNs, transformers) and little cores handle diffusion model iterative steps; heterogeneous compute fabric scales performance and energy across workload diversity.

title: 11.4 A Gm-C RF Quadrature-Current-Generation Technique with 40dB IRR in 0.65V 2mW Multi-Mode CMOS GNSS Receiver
problem: Signal-quadrature receiver topologies offer power efficiency over LO-quadrature designs but suffer from poor I/Q phase and amplitude accuracy due to parasitic capacitances and impedances that are difficult to calibrate when using signal-engaged switches.
method: A Gm-C (transconductance-capacitive) RF quadrature-current-generation technique that derives orthogonal I and Q signals directly from the RF signal using transconductor circuits rather than passive switches. This approach reduces parasitic sensitivity and enables robust phase/amplitude balance calibration.

title: SmoothE: Differentiable E-Graph Extraction
problem: E-graph extraction—selecting the optimal expression from a compact equality-saturation graph—suffers from an unfavorable scalability-quality trade-off: exact methods are slow, and fast heuristics produce suboptimal results. Current methods also only support simple linear cost functions, limiting applicability to realistic optimization objectives (e.g., non-linear, learned cost models).
method: SmoothE formulates e-graph extraction as a continuous, differentiable optimization problem by relaxing the discrete, combinatorial node-selection problem to a smooth objective over real-valued weights. Gradient-based optimization (e.g., gradient descent) is then applied to find the optimal extraction, enabling the use of arbitrary differentiable cost functions including learned neural cost models. The relaxation is designed so that the continuous optimum closely corresponds to a valid discrete extraction.

title: 20.4 MEMS-Free 4096-Pixel CMOS E-Nose Gas-Sensor Array with Molecular-Selective Metal-Organic-Framework Sensing and In-Pixel Thermodynamic Modulation for Fast Sensor Regeneration
problem: Electronic noses lack sufficient sensor selectivity, suffer from sensor memory effects due to slow gas desorption, and have small sensor arrays without in-pixel processing, limiting real-time gas detection in industrial and safety applications.
method: Monolithic CMOS integration of 4096 molecular-selective MOF (metal-organic-framework) sensors with in-pixel temperature regulation enabling thermodynamic control of gas adsorption/desorption, coupled with local readout and digitization circuits.

title: 18.5 A Rail-to-Rail 3rd-Order Noise-Shaping SAR ADC Achieving 105.4dB SFDR with Integrated Input Buffer Using Continuous-Time Correlated Level Shifting
problem: High-resolution SAR ADCs (>13b) require large capacitive DACs to meet kT/C noise specs, heavily loading the input buffer. Buffer driving large CDAC while achieving rail-to-rail swing and linearity dominates power consumption, becoming the efficiency bottleneck.
method: Rail-to-rail SAR ADC with continuous-time correlated level shifting in the input buffer, integrating the buffer into the noise-shaping loop. Level shifting bias compensates for signal swing while maintaining linearity, avoiding need for higher supply voltage.

title: 6.8 A Real-Time Pixel-Compensated Source-Driver IC with Dual-Slope Error Detection and Multi-Channel Time-Multiplexing Compensator for Compact OLED Displays
problem: LTPS-TFT OLED displays suffer from pixel-to-pixel variations in DTFT parameters (Kp, Vth) and channel-wise voltage offsets (Vos), causing non-uniform drain current and luminance even with identical input data. Internal compensation via additional TFTs/capacitors reduces aperture ratio and efficiency.
method: A source-driver IC implements external real-time pixel compensation: (1) dual-slope error detection measures DTFT characteristics per pixel, (2) multi-channel time-multiplexed compensator dynamically adjusts Vdata for each pixel to correct current/luminance variation, (3) external approach preserves pixel aperture ratio vs. internal compensation.

title: SEAL: A Single-Event Architecture for In-Sensor Visual Localization
problem: Traditional binary-encoded image sensors generate large data volumes that create energy and latency bottlenecks during transfer, storage, and processing for visual localization tasks such as keypoint detection and tracking. Moving these operations off-sensor to a host processor adds significant latency and energy cost.
method: SEAL introduces delay-based (temporal) codes at the pixel array level, replacing binary encoding with analog-to-time converters (ATCs) that represent pixel values as pulse delays (race logic). A temporal processor co-designed with the ATCs implements keypoint detection and tracking using race logic's single-wire-per-variable, single-event-per-wire policy, maximizing energy and area efficiency. A heavily quantized frontend processor then processes temporal outputs before the sensor-processor interface, enabling in-sensor VIO pipeline stages.

title: 27.5: A 4, 100µm2 Wire-Metal-Based Temperature Sensor with a Fractional-Discharge FLL and a Time-Domain Amplifier with ±0.2°C Inaccuracy (3σ) from -40 to 125°C and 45fJ·K2 Resolution FoM in 28nm CMOS
problem: Resistance-based temperature sensors must achieve compact area (<5000µm²), high accuracy (±0.2°C, 3σ), and superior resolution FoM while operating across wide temperature ranges in advanced low-VDD processes.
method: Resistor-based temperature sensor using wire-metal sensing element with fractional-discharge FLL (frequency-locked loop) and time-domain amplifier for sensitive measurement, eliminating biasing constraints of active-device sensors.

title: Measurement-based uncomputation of quantum circuits for modular arithmetic
problem: Quantum circuits for modular arithmetic suffer from high Toffoli gate counts and circuit depths, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained quantum systems.
method: Applies measurement-based uncomputation (MBU) technique to single-qubit registers performing modular arithmetic. MBU enables probabilistic uncomputation by leveraging measurement outcomes to reduce gate overhead. The approach is formalized for modular arithmetic operations and validated on different modular adder architectures.

title: LSQCA: Resource-Efficient Load/Store Architecture for Limited-Scale Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
problem: Current fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) floorplan strategies devote 50% of qubit memory space to routing/overhead required for unit-time random access to all logical qubits, leaving only half the qubit count available for data storage when qubits are scarce.
method: LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) separates logical qubit memory into Computational Registers (CR), a small fast-access region, and Scan-Access Memory (SAM), a dense storage region accessed with variable latency. An instruction set is defined over these abstractions, with concrete implementations as point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. Access latency in SAM is hidden by overlapping it with other computational bottlenecks, exploiting access locality patterns identified through static analysis of quantum program memory reference timestamps. Optimization techniques leverage locality in memory reference ordering to further reduce effective latency penalties.

title: A 28nm 18.1μJ /Acquisition End-to-End GPS Acquisition Accelerator with Energy-Accuracy-Driven Mixed-Radix IFFT and ROM-Assisted Computing
problem: GPS receiver acquisition is the most energy-consuming task in mobile GNSS receivers, requiring correlation of multi-satellite signals across Doppler range and code delay space. Conventional implementations perform full IFFT/FFT per satellite at high precision, consuming significant energy; accuracy-vs-energy tradeoff is not exploited during algorithm optimization.
method: Energy-accuracy-driven mixed-radix IFFT reduces precision dynamically based on Doppler and code-delay estimation stages (early stages tolerate lower precision). ROM-assisted computing replaces iterative multiplications with precomputed lookup tables where precision requirements are low. 28nm CMOS accelerator integrates dual NCO (numerically controlled oscillator), mixed-radix FFT engine, and correlator with adaptive word-widths.

title: 3.3 A Passive Switched-Capacitor-Based Multimode Amplifier with a Logarithmic Conformity Error of 0.75% from -25 to 200°C
problem: Harsh geothermal and high-temperature environments (up to 200°C) require sensor front-end amplifiers with wide dynamic range (>80dB), low temperature drift, and accurate phase/amplitude across extreme temperature spans. Existing logarithmic amplifiers exhibit high temperature dependence; low-drift amplifiers require complex trimming and compensation.
method: A passive switched-capacitor (SC) topology with multimode operation achieves high dynamic range and temperature stability. The design leverages discrete-time SC amplification to improve noise efficiency while avoiding the thermal drift issues of traditional logarithmic or low-drift amplifiers, using novel compensation mechanisms for stability across -25 to 200°C.
